reference.source: Paediatric endocrinology and clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Presents with congenital hypoparathyroidism and neonatal hypocalcaemic seizures or tetany.
Autosomal recessive and caused by TBCE variants, with a strong founder effect in consanguineous Arab and other Middle Eastern kindreds.
Comprises the triad of hypoparathyroidism, severe pre- and postnatal growth retardation and dysmorphism (the hypoparathyroidism-retardation-dysmorphism, or HRD, phenotype).
Characteristic facies include microcephaly, deep-set eyes, a thin beaked nose, thin upper lip, micrognathia and large low-set ears.
Intellectual disability and small hands and feet are typical.
Allelic to Kenny-Caffey syndrome type 1 (also TBCE), which is distinguished by medullary stenosis of the long bones and comparatively preserved development.
Recurrent infections and failure to thrive are common, and intercurrent illness can precipitate hypocalcaemic crises.
Management is lifelong calcium and active vitamin D analogues such as alfacalcidol or calcitriol, with monitoring for hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Sanjad-Sakati syndrome is an autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in TBCE, which encodes a tubulin-specific chaperone required for the correct folding of alpha-tubulin and for microtubule assembly. A founder deletion is highly prevalent in Arab and other Middle Eastern populations with consanguinity. Defective microtubule function impairs parathyroid gland embryogenesis, producing parathyroid aplasia or hypoplasia and hence congenital hypoparathyroidism, while also disrupting intrauterine and postnatal growth and neurodevelopment. Deficient parathyroid hormone secretion leads to hypocalcaemia with hyperphosphataemia, which manifests in the neonatal period as tetany and seizures and over time may cause basal ganglia calcification. The condition is allelic to autosomal recessive Kenny-Caffey syndrome type 1, which shares TBCE variants but is distinguished by medullary stenosis of the long bones and relatively preserved cognition.
additionalDifferentials: Mitochondrial disorders with hypoparathyroidism such as Kearns-Sayre syndrome
Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (AIRE) with hypoparathyroidism
Barakat (HDR) syndrome with hypoparathyroidism, deafness and renal dysplasia (GATA3)
Isolated familial hypoparathyroidism (GCM2, PTH or activating CASR variants)
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium (low), phosphate (raised) and parathyroid hormone (inappropriately low or undetectable)
Serum magnesium and vitamin D status
Renal ultrasound at baseline and for monitoring of nephrocalcinosis
Skeletal survey to look for the medullary stenosis that characterises Kenny-Caffey syndrome
Developmental and neurological assessment with brain imaging for basal ganglia calcification
Molecular testing of TBCE, including the recognised founder variant
redFlags: Neonatal seizures due to severe hypocalcaemia
Laryngospasm, stridor or cardiac arrhythmia from hypocalcaemia
Serious infection or sepsis, to which affected infants are susceptible
Progressive neurological deterioration with basal ganglia calcification
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is guarded, with significant early mortality from hypocalcaemic seizures, infections and failure to thrive; survivors have persistent short stature and intellectual disability and need lifelong multidisciplinary care.
pitfalls: Attributing neonatal seizures to hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and overlooking hypocalcaemia and hypoparathyroidism
Over-replacement with calcium and vitamin D causing hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis
Confusing the condition with DiGeorge syndrome without checking 22q11.2 status and immune and cardiac features
Failing to recognise the founder variant in consanguineous families, delaying genetic diagnosis
Not distinguishing it from Kenny-Caffey syndrome, which shows skeletal medullary stenosis
references: Clinical genetics references on hereditary hypoparathyroidism syndromes
Standard references on metabolic bone disease
management: Lifelong treatment of the congenital hypoparathyroidism with oral calcium and an active vitamin D analogue such as alfacalcidol or calcitriol
Emergency intravenous calcium for hypocalcaemic tetany or seizures in the neonatal period and during crises
Correction of coexisting magnesium deficiency, which can impair the response to calcium replacement
Serial monitoring of calcium, phosphate and renal function, with renal ultrasound surveillance for nephrocalcinosis from therapy
Nutritional support and active management of failure to thrive, with prompt aggressive treatment of intercurrent infections
Developmental support and neurological monitoring, including brain imaging for basal ganglia calcification
Coordinated care through paediatric endocrinology, clinical genetics and allied services
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive TBCE disorder, with founder-variant testing and family screening in consanguineous kindreds
